options.text: Anyone who might buy the product
A specific group sharing a need or characteristic
The person who pays the most
A business's competitors

questions.explanation: A target customer is a defined group who share a characteristic — such as age, location or lifestyle — that makes them likely to need what you sell. 'Everyone' is not a target customer.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 8–12 on identifying customers and market research

questions.stem: A customer need is the same thing as a product feature.
questions.explanation: A customer need is the problem or want seen from the customer's perspective. A product feature is how the product addresses it. For example, 'not enough time to cook' is a need; 'ready in 5 minutes' is a feature.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 8–12 on customer needs and wants

questions.stem: A student writes: 'My business will make money by helping people.' What is missing?

options.text: A business name
A specific product or service
A financial plan
A marketing strategy

questions.explanation: A business idea must state concretely what the business sells — a specific product or service. 'Helping people' is too vague to be a business idea.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 5–8 on business activity and enterprise

questions.stem: What does 'linking the product to the customer need' mean?

options.text: Listing all the features of the product
Explaining how the product solves the customer's specific problem
Setting a competitive price
Advertising the product on social media

questions.explanation: The link connects the product to the customer's need: it explains WHY this product solves THIS customer's problem. It is not about features, pricing, or promotion on their own.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 8–12 on understanding customer needs

questions.stem: 'Everyone aged 10 to 80' is a well-defined target customer group.
questions.explanation: A target customer must have at least one distinguishing characteristic. A range covering almost everyone is effectively the same as saying 'everyone' — it is not specific enough.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 8–12 on identifying customers and market research

questions.stem: Match each example to the correct part of a business idea.

pairs.left: Busy parents who need last-minute gifts

questions.explanation: A complete business idea names a product, identifies a specific customer with a need, and explains how the product meets that need.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 5–12 on business ideas and enterprise

questions.stem: Which of these is a customer NEED rather than a product feature?

options.text: Made from organic ingredients
Available in three sizes
Parents struggle to find healthy school lunches
Delivered within 24 hours

questions.explanation: A customer need describes a problem or want from the customer's point of view. The other options are product features — things the product does. The need is the reason the customer would care about those features.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 8–12 on customer needs and wants

questions.stem: Which business idea is specific enough?

options.text: A shop that sells stuff to people
An online tutoring service for Year 11 maths students in Adelaide
A business that makes money online
Something with food for hungry people

questions.explanation: Option B names a specific service (online tutoring), a subject (maths), a customer group (Year 11 students), and a location (Adelaide). The others are too vague about what is sold or who buys it.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 5–12 on business ideas and enterprise

questions.stem: Saying 'my product is good because it is cheap' is enough to show the link between product and customer need.
questions.explanation: A link must explain how the product meets a specific customer's need. 'It is cheap' describes a feature but does not say which need it solves or for whom. The link must go from customer need to product, not just list a feature.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 8–12 on understanding customer needs

questions.stem: A student says their target customers are 'elderly residents in a retirement village who find it hard to cook meals.' Which parts are present?

options.text: Only a customer group
Only a customer need
Both a specific customer group and a need
Neither — it is too vague

questions.explanation: The customer group is specific (elderly residents in a retirement village — defined by age and location). The need is stated from their perspective (finding it hard to cook meals). Both elements are present.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 8–12 on customer needs and wants
